unit.title: Computational thinking, unplugged and with blocks

video.title: Algorithms: Exact instructions, in order
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Amina at the board with a tiny square drawn in its corner; her class laughing.
scenes.narration: I asked my class how to draw a house, and they said: draw a square. So I drew a tiny square, in the corner of the board! They laughed, but they had just found out what a computer needs.
Today: algorithms, and why instructions must be exact.
An algorithm is a list of steps that solves a problem. Each step is precise, the steps come in order, and the list finishes. A recipe is an algorithm. So are the directions to the market.
A program is an algorithm written for a computer. The computer does exactly what each step says, and nothing more. It can’t guess what you meant. So draw a square isn’t enough: how big, and where?
Algorithms are all around a school. The steps of long division. The fire drill. Making tea for the staffroom. Each one works only if the steps are clear and in the right order.

Think of giving directions to a visitor who has never been to your town. Turn left at the market, but which corner? Walk a little way, but how far? Good directions, like good algorithms, leave nothing to guess.
Quick check! I want a robot to make tea. Which instructions can it follow?
The numbered list. A robot can’t fill the gaps the way a person can. Every step must be clear, and in the right order. You can’t pour the tea before you boil the water.

Here is a robot on a grid. It understands only three commands: forward one square, turn left and turn right. Turning doesn’t move it; it only changes the way it faces. To reach the target, you put the commands in the exact order.

You don’t need a device for this. Chalk a grid on the floor, and one pupil is the robot. The class holds up arrow cards, one at a time. The robot does exactly what each card says, even if it walks into a wall.
In the app, open Program a robot. Lay the command cards in order, then press Run and watch it walk. Start with grids one to three.
Your turn. My robot faces up, and the target is one square up and one to the right. Which program gets it there?

scenes.on_screen_text: Precise · In order · Exactly what you say
scenes.narration: Forward, turn right, forward. Remember: an algorithm is precise steps, in order, that finish. A computer does exactly what you say, not what you mean. And you can teach it all with chalk, cards and a pupil robot.
Try it in class tomorrow: play Human robot. Chalk a grid, choose a robot, and let the class guide it to a target with arrow cards, one card at a time. When it goes wrong, ask: which card was the bug?

checkpoints.prompt: Which instructions can a robot follow to make tea?

options.text: A numbered list of exact steps
Any words: it will work it out

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a robot can’t fill gaps, so every step must be exact and in order.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a robot does only what each step says. It needs a numbered list of exact steps.

checkpoints.prompt: The robot faces up; the target is one square up and one right. Which program works?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — up one square, turn to face right, then one more square.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — order matters. Up one, turn right, then forward one more.
